title: The Sharpe Pint: The Memory Tax, Trillion-Dollar Chicken, and the McNamara Trap

opening_mood.text: Morning. If you have looked at your portfolio this morning and wondered why the tech-heavy green has turned into a rather bruised shade of red, you can thank the physical world. It turns out AI isn't just code floating in the ether; it requires actual silicon, copper, and a staggering amount of memory chips.
Grab a pint (or a very strong espresso), and let's unpack the 'memory tax' hitting Apple, Sam Altman's game of valuation chicken, and why your spreadsheets might be lying to you.

content.text: The Memory Tax: Apple and Microsoft Hike Prices as AI Capex Bites

If you wanted proof that the AI boom isn't just a software fairy tale, look no further than your next hardware upgrade. Apple has announced price increases on iPads and MacBooks, blaming surging memory and storage chip costs driven by insatiable AI demand. Microsoft followed suit, slapping up to $150 onto Xbox consoles. The market's reaction was swift and brutal: Apple shares tumbled 6.1%, wiping out a cool $263 billion in market cap overnight and triggering a massive sell-off across Asian tech hubs, with South Korea's Kospi diving 6.9%.

Why it matters: We've spent the last two years marvelling at Nvidia's eye-watering margins, but we're now seeing the flip side of the coin. The physical cost of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and advanced storage—supplied by the likes of Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron—is acting as a tax on consumer tech giants. Instead of AI driving pure margin expansion, hardware manufacturers are being forced to choose between eating the margin squeeze or testing consumer price elasticity.

The City angle: For asset managers, this is a classic supply chain margin squeeze. The key question is whether Apple can pass these costs on without killing volume. If consumer demand falters, the high-flying valuations of consumer tech giants look incredibly vulnerable.

items: What to say at the pub: "Everyone's been obsessed with Nvidia's margins, but the real story is the memory tax. When Apple has to hike iPad prices and takes a 6% hit to its stock, it shows the physical limits of the AI capex boom are hitting consumer pockets."

Interview talking point: Discuss how supply chain bottlenecks in the semiconductor space (specifically memory) are shifting the profit pool from device assemblers and software platforms to hardware component manufacturers.

content.text: Sam Altman's $1 Trillion Game of Chicken: OpenAI IPO Slipped to 2027

OpenAI is reportedly leaning toward delaying its highly anticipated IPO until 2027. The reason? CEO Sam Altman is playing a game of valuation chicken, refusing to go public at anything less than a $1 trillion valuation (a massive step up from its last private round of $730 billion). Advisers reportedly gave Altman a choice: go public in 2027 at the trillion-dollar mark, or accept a lower valuation for a quicker listing. Altman's response? Anything below a trillion is a 'nonstarter'. The news sent SoftBank—one of OpenAI's biggest backers—tumbling 13% in a single day.

Why it matters: The public markets are no longer a private VC playground. The primary catalyst for the delay was SpaceX's rocky post-IPO performance earlier this month; despite a record-breaking debut at a $1.77 trillion valuation, Elon Musk's rocket company saw its stock slide from a peak of $202 to $153. Public investors are starting to demand actual unit economics and ROI on AI, rather than just buying into the hype of slowing ChatGPT user growth and heavy operational losses.

The City angle: For investment bankers and growth equity investors, this is a clear signal that the mega-tech IPO window is getting much more selective. It also highlights the growing valuation gap between private funding rounds and public market realities.

items: What to say at work: "Altman's $1 trillion ultimatum is a massive gamble. SpaceX's post-IPO drop shows that public investors will actually look at the unit economics. If OpenAI waits until 2027, they're betting they can turn ChatGPT's slowing user growth into a money-printing machine before then."
Interview talking point: Analyse the divergence between private venture valuations and public market pricing, using OpenAI and SpaceX as case studies for late-stage liquidity challenges.

content.text: OpenAI Poaches Apple's Vision Pro Chief for Hardware Push

In a move that signals its ambitions extend far beyond software, OpenAI has poached Paul Meade, Apple's VP of hardware engineering for the Vision Pro and smart glasses. Meade will reportedly head up OpenAI's in-house hardware division, tasked with building a family of AI-first physical devices. His departure comes amid a wider restructuring at Apple under new chief hardware officer Johny Srouji, as John Ternus prepares to take over as CEO from Tim Cook on September 1.

Why it matters: OpenAI is clearly tired of being a mere software layer on Apple's iOS. By building its own hardware ecosystem—potentially smart glasses or wearables—OpenAI hopes to bypass the App Store tax and create a vertically integrated AI giant. It already acquired Jony Ive's hardware startup for $6.5 billion last year, and Meade's hire suggests they are ready to turn those design concepts into physical reality.

The City angle: The battle for the next computing platform is heating up. If OpenAI can successfully launch a hardware device, it threatens the hardware dominance of Apple and Meta. For tech analysts, this is a major strategic shift to watch.

items: What to say over a pint: "OpenAI poaching Apple's Vision Pro hardware chief is a massive statement of intent. They aren't content being a software layer on Apple's iOS; they want to own the physical device itself. With Jony Ive already in the fold, they're building a formidable hardware team."
Interview talking point: Discuss the strategic rationale of vertical integration in the AI space, and how owning the hardware layer can protect an AI company's moat against platform risk.

content.text: Nasdaq Smashes Records in $334 Billion Russell Reconstitution

On June 26, the Nasdaq Closing Cross executed a record-breaking 4.59 billion shares worth $334 billion in just 1.63 seconds. The massive liquidity event was driven by the semi-annual rebalancing of the Russell US Indexes, which includes the Russell 1000, 2000, and 3000. This milestone easily surpassed the 2025 reconstitution, which saw $102 billion executed.

Why it matters: This is a testament to the sheer scale of passive investing. With over $10.6 trillion in assets benchmarked to the Russell indexes, any shift in market capitalisation or sector dominance triggers massive, instantaneous flows. The fact that Nasdaq's infrastructure can handle a third of a trillion dollars in under two seconds is a marvel of modern market microstructure.

The City angle: For quants, market makers, and execution traders, the Russell Reconstitution is the ultimate test of execution algorithms. Getting a clean fill at the close is critical to avoiding tracking error, and the record volume shows that liquidity is becoming increasingly concentrated in these scheduled index events.

items: What to say at work: "Executing $334 billion in 1.63 seconds is an incredible feat of market infrastructure. It shows how dominant passive flows have become. If you're a quant or execution trader, this is the Super Bowl of liquidity events."
Interview talking point: Explain the mechanics of index reconstitution and how passive fund flows impact market liquidity and price discovery at the close.

content.text: FDIC Throws a Bone to Mid-Sized Banks: Streamlining 'Living Wills'

The FDIC Board of Directors has approved a proposal to raise the asset threshold for 'living wills' (resolution plans) from $50 billion to $100 billion, exempting 16 of the 48 banks currently covered. The proposal also slashes content requirements by more than half, eliminating the need for extensive hypothetical analyses, and moves banks to a three-year filing cycle.

Why it matters: This is a major regulatory relief for mid-sized US banks, reducing compliance costs and bureaucratic red tape. FDIC Chairman Travis Hill noted that the historical approach of demanding lengthy narrative plans was ineffective, and the new rule focuses purely on the key information needed to execute a resolution.

The City angle: For bank analysts and investors, this is a clear positive for regional bank margins. It reduces the regulatory burden that has plagued mid-cap banks since the 2023 banking crisis, allowing them to focus on actual risk management rather than compliance theatre.

items: What to say over a pint: "The FDIC raising the threshold to $100 billion is a massive win for regional banks. It cuts out the compliance theatre of writing 1,000-page 'living wills' that nobody reads, allowing mid-sized banks to focus on actual risk management rather than regulatory box-ticking."
Interview talking point: Discuss the balance between financial stability and regulatory burden, and how streamlining resolution plans can improve the efficiency of the banking sector.

content.text: Blue Owl Spreads Its Wings: Shareholders Approve $2.4B Sila REIT Buyout

Shareholders of Sila Realty Trust, a healthcare REIT, have overwhelmingly approved its $2.4 billion all-cash acquisition by Blue Owl Capital. The deal, which offers Sila stockholders $30.38 per share in cash, is set to close on July 1, 2026, taking Sila private and delisting it from the NYSE.

Why it matters: Blue Owl is aggressively expanding its real estate and real assets footprint. Healthcare real estate (medical offices, senior housing) is seen as a highly resilient, defensive asset class in a volatile macro environment, offering predictable, durable income streams.

The City angle: Private equity and alternative asset managers are continuing to deploy massive dry powder into defensive real estate. This is a classic 'triple-net lease' play where the tenant pays all operating expenses, providing highly predictable cash flows that are attractive in a high-interest-rate environment.

items: What to say at work: "Blue Owl's $2.4 billion buyout of Sila shows that alternative asset managers are still hungry for defensive yield. Healthcare REITs are the ultimate defensive play—highly resilient demand, long-term leases, and inflation protection."
Interview talking point: Explain the strategic rationale behind private equity firms acquiring public REITs, focusing on the valuation gap and the benefits of taking real estate assets private.

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: It was a jittery week in the City and on Wall Street, with the S&P 500 halting a four-day slide on Friday to close almost flat (-0.05% at 7,354.02), while the tech-heavy Nasdaq slipped -0.24%. For the week as a whole, the Nasdaq was thoroughly battered, down -4.48%, while the S&P 500 shed -1.96%. Meanwhile, the Dow Jones Industrial Average managed a modest +0.62% weekly gain. What we are looking at is a classic, aggressive rotation out of high-flying tech and chipmakers into value and defensives. Speculative froth is being scraped off the top, and the market is demanding some cold, hard mathematical reality.
The AI Tax and Trillion-Dollar Cold Feet

The big story of the week is that the massive capital expenditure on AI is finally hitting the consumer's wallet—and tech giants are blinking. First, Apple and Microsoft dropped a bombshell by raising hardware prices, blaming 'unprecedented' surges in memory chip costs driven by AI data centre demand. Apple hiked prices on MacBooks and iPads by up to 20% (the budget MacBook Neo jumped from $599 to $699, and the iPad Air rose to $749). Microsoft followed suit by raising Xbox console prices. This 'AI tax' shows that the physical limits of the AI buildout—specifically RAM and storage shortages—are starting to squeeze hardware margins, forcing tech firms to pass the bill directly to consumers.

To make matters worse for the tech bulls, OpenAI is reportedly getting cold feet about its highly anticipated public debut. Just weeks after filing confidential S-1 paperwork, advisors are urging Sam Altman to delay the IPO until 2027. Why? Because they just watched Elon Musk's SpaceX (SPCX) IPO go from a $2 trillion intraday high on June 17 to tumbling back to $152.86 on Friday—almost wiping out its post-listing gains. With Altman reportedly treating a $1 trillion valuation as a 'non-starter,' bankers are terrified that public market retail demand is simply too exhausted to absorb another massive narrative-driven listing. When a startup is private, it can survive on the romantic projections of venture capitalists; the public market, however, demands immediate, transparent execution.
Warsh's 'Vol-Thunderdome' and the New Fed

In the rates space, the 10-year US Treasury yield is hovering around 4.39% as the market continues to digest the radical regime change at the Federal Reserve. Newly minted Fed Chair Kevin Warsh used his first FOMC meeting on June 17 to completely demolish the old communication playbook. Warsh kept rates steady at 3.50% - 3.75% but ditched forward guidance entirely, calling it 'not well-suited to the current policy conjuncture.' He shortened the statement, refused to submit his own dot-plot projections, and left the market to figure things out based on raw data. With US CPI flaring to 4.2% in May due to the earlier energy shock from the Iran war, the dot plot leaned hawkish, with several members signaling rate hikes later this year. For traders, the message is clear: the era of central bank hand-holding is over. Welcome to the data-dependent 'Vol-thunderdome.'
Crude Realities and Shaky Ceasefires

Commodities had a wild ride, with WTI crude oil futures plunging -8.14% on the week (-3.1% on Friday). On paper, the drop is driven by the US-Iran Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed on June 17, which formalised a ceasefire and aimed to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. But the reality on the water is incredibly messy. On Friday, US and Iranian forces traded military strikes after a commercial vessel was struck off the coast of Oman. Donald Trump took to social media to threaten the 'annihilation' of Iran if the ceasefire is violated. Yet, oil traders are looking past the theatrical sabre-rattling; as long as traffic continues to flow through the Strait, the geopolitical risk premium is being aggressively priced out. Precious metals also took a beating, with gold futures down -2.43% on the week and spot silver tumbling -10.83%.
The Cross-Asset Read: What's Underneath the Surface?

If you look underneath the hood, the cross-asset picture is telling us that the 'narrative-only' phase of the market cycle is hitting a hard ceiling. The US dollar rose +0.58% on the week, supported by high real rates and a hawkish Fed, while Bitcoin fell -6.3% as speculative liquidity dried up. On Friday, the Nasdaq Closing Cross saw a record-breaking $334 billion executed in just 1.63 seconds for the Russell Reconstitution, showing that institutional liquidity is still massive, but it is actively repositioning. The lesson for anyone in asset management or banking is simple: when the world's most valuable company (Apple) has to raise prices because of physical supply constraints, and the poster child of AI (OpenAI) delays its public listing because the public market demands actual mathematical execution over VC romance, we are transitioning from 'hype' to 'balance sheet reality.'

content.text: The DTL Dilemma: Is a Deferred Tax Liability Actually Debt?

If you’ve ever built an Enterprise Value (EV) to Equity Value bridge for an LBO model, or argued over a completion accounts mechanism in a transaction, you’ve likely run into Deferred Tax Liabilities (DTLs). They sit there on the liability side of the balance sheet, looking suspiciously like debt. But treating them as such can cost you—or your client—millions. Let’s break down why DTLs are the ultimate "it depends" of corporate finance.
What is a DTL anyway?

At its core, a DTL is just a timing difference between book accounting (what you show shareholders) and tax accounting (what you show HMRC). The classic culprit is accelerated depreciation. Say a company buys a 10m machine. HMRC might let them write off 100% of it in Year 1 to encourage investment (e.g., via full expensing). But for the book accounts, the company depreciates it straight-line over 5 years (2m a year).

items: Year 1 Book Depreciation: 2m
Year 1 Tax Depreciation: 10m
The difference: 8m of "untaxed" book profit.

At a 25% tax rate, that’s 2m of tax the company has saved today, but will theoretically have to pay back over the next four years as book depreciation continues without any tax offsets. That 2m is your DTL.

content.text: The Great M&A Debate: Debt or Equity?

In a transaction, the buyer and seller argue over "debt-like items" to adjust the purchase price. The buyer wants to classify everything possible as debt (reducing the cash paid to the seller). The seller wants the opposite. So, is a DTL debt?
The answer depends entirely on the future of the business:

items: The Going Concern (Permanent Capital): If the company is growing and constantly buying new machines, it will keep generating new DTLs faster than the old ones unwind. The total DTL balance on the balance sheet will keep growing. In this case, the tax is never actually paid back. It is effectively interest-free, permanent capital. Treating it as debt is a massive mistake that unfairly penalises the seller.

The Run-off (Real Cash Drain): If the company stops investing, or if you are buying it to wind it down, those timing differences will reverse. The cash tax bill will spike over the next few years. In this scenario, the DTL is a very real, looming cash liability and absolutely should be treated as debt.

content.text: The Rookie Mistake: The PPA Trap

There is one type of DTL you should never treat as debt: the Purchase Price Allocation (PPA) DTL. When a company is acquired, the accountants write up the value of intangible assets (like brand names or customer relationships). Because these written-up assets are amortised in the book accounts but are not tax-deductible, a massive DTL is created on the balance sheet to balance the books.

This PPA DTL is a pure accounting phantom. It will only ever "unwind" as non-cash book amortisation. It will never, under any circumstances, result in a single penny of cash leaving the company to pay tax. Treating a PPA DTL as a debt-like item in a valuation is an instant way to get laughed out of an investment committee.
How to use this in interviews and at work

If you are interviewing for private equity or corporate finance, this is a classic differentiator question. When asked "How do you treat DTLs in an EV bridge?", don't just say "you add them to debt." Instead, show some commercial teeth:

items: The Smart Answer: "It depends on the capital expenditure cycle. If the company is in steady-state or growth capex, the DTL rolls over and acts as interest-free financing, so we exclude it. If capex is dropping off, it’s a real cash drain, so we treat it as debt-like. And I’d always exclude any PPA-related DTLs because they never trigger cash taxes."

Over a Pint: "Honestly, calling a growing company's DTL 'debt' is just a cheeky way for PE buyers to shave 5% off the purchase price. If the seller has a decent advisor, they’ll spot it in five minutes."

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day

content.text: The Death of the Expected Value: Distributional RL in Finance

If you have ever sat through a pitch from an AI startup promising to "revolutionise" trading using Reinforcement Learning (RL), you have probably felt a familiar twitch in your eye. Most off-the-shelf RL algorithms are built on a fundamental lie when it comes to finance: they only care about the expected value (the mean) of the reward. In the real world, optimising solely for the average return is a fast track to the career graveyard. If you have a strategy with a 99% win rate that occasionally suffers a catastrophic 100% loss, standard RL thinks it is a stellar bet. Your risk manager, however, will have you escorted from the building before lunchtime.

This is where Distributional Reinforcement Learning (DRL) comes in. Instead of collapsing the future into a single, comfortable average, DRL forces the agent to model the entire probability distribution of potential outcomes. It does not just ask "What is my expected return?" It asks "What does the left tail look like, and how likely am I to blow up?"
The Finance Use Case: Hedging Autocallables and Tail Risk

Consider hedging a portfolio of complex structured products, like Autocallable notes. These are notoriously tricky beasts. They have built-in barriers that trigger coupon payments or early redemption, meaning their payoff profiles have massive, non-linear discontinuities. If the underlying asset drops past a barrier, your delta changes instantly and violently. Standard RL agents trained on average PnL get absolutely slaughtered here because they are blind to the tail risk. In a recent paper, "Hedging Beyond the Mean" (Sharma et al., 2024), researchers showed that by using Distributional RL, an agent can learn to hedge structured products far more effectively, explicitly minimising Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) and keeping the left tail of the PnL distribution firmly under control.
Under the Hood: Quantile Regression DQN (QR-DQN)

How does it work under the hood? In a standard Deep Q-Network (DQN), the neural network outputs a single scalar representing the expected future reward for taking an action. In a Quantile Regression DQN (QR-DQN), the network outputs a vector of N quantiles (say, 51 different percentiles from the 1st to the 99th). This gives the agent a complete picture of the probability density function of the return. When it is time to act, instead of just picking the action with the highest average, we can instruct the agent to pick the action that maximises a risk-adjusted metric, like the average of the worst 10% of outcomes (the CVaR).

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class QRDQN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, state_dim, action_dim, num_quantiles=51):
        super().__init__()
        self.num_quantiles = num_quantiles
        self.action_dim = action_dim
        # Network outputs (action_dim * num_quantiles)
        self.fc = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(state_dim, 128),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(128, action_dim * num_quantiles)
        )
        
    def forward(self, state):
        # Shape: [batch_size, action_dim, num_quantiles]
        out = self.fc(state)
        return out.view(-1, self.action_dim, self.num_quantiles)

def select_action_cvar(state, model, alpha=0.1):
    """
    Selects the action that maximises the Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR)
    at level alpha (the average of the worst alpha-percentile of outcomes).
    """
    state_t = torch.FloatTensor(state).unsqueeze(0)
    with torch.no_grad():
        quantiles = model(state_t).squeeze(0).numpy()
        
    num_quantiles = quantiles.shape[1]
    cutoff_idx = max(1, int(alpha * num_quantiles))
    
    cvar_per_action = []
    for action_idx in range(quantiles.shape[0]):
        # Sort the quantiles for this action
        sorted_q = np.sort(quantiles[action_idx])
        # CVaR is the average of the worst alpha-percentile
        cvar = np.mean(sorted_q[:cutoff_idx])
        cvar_per_action.append(cvar)
        
    return np.argmax(cvar_per_action)
The Interview & Pub Angle

In your next interview or team meeting, when someone inevitably suggests using RL for portfolio allocation or execution, you can drop this: "Standard RL is fundamentally risk-blind because it only optimises for the expected value. If you are deploying RL in a highly stochastic, asymmetric environment like options hedging or block execution, you have to look at Distributional RL. By outputting the full quantile distribution of the Q-value, you can bake risk measures like CVaR directly into the action selection. It is the difference between an agent that chases yield off a cliff and one that actually respects the downside."
The Catch (Because There's Always a Catch)

items: Sample Efficiency: Learning a full distribution (e.g., 51 or 100 quantiles) requires significantly more data and training time than learning a single scalar, which exacerbates the sample-efficiency problem in finance.

Non-stationarity: If the market regime shifts, your learned quantiles will be completely wrong. The agent might think its worst-case loss is -5% based on training data, but a black swan event will still catch it completely off guard.

Time Inconsistency: As highlighted in a recent ICLR 2026 paper ("What Distributional Reinforcement Learning is Learning?"), using dynamic risk measures like CVaR in sequential decision-making introduces 'time inconsistency'—meaning an action that looks optimal today might not look optimal tomorrow, which plays havoc with the mathematical convergence of the model.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: Right, grab a pint and let's talk about the Fed. No, don't run away—this isn't another dry speech on terminal rates. It's actually a brilliant bit of research where central bankers let Large Language Models loose in a classic behavioural finance lab.
The Paper
Financial Stability Implications of Generative AI: Taming the Animal Spirits by Anne Lundgaard Hansen and Seung Jung Lee (Federal Reserve Board of Governors, FEDS Working Paper 2025-090).
Why This One?

Most central bank papers on AI are hand-wringing policy pieces about 'operational resilience' or 'cyber risks'—essentially, dry corporate waffle. This one is different. The authors actually set up a laboratory-style experiment using LLMs to replicate classic economic studies on herd behaviour. It’s a rare, rigorous look at how AI agents actually make decisions when placed in a market simulation, and what that means for the future of market stability.
The Setup

The researchers used a classic sequential trading game (the Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer, and Welch model from 1992). In this game, players make investment decisions one after the other. Each player gets a private signal (e.g., 'the asset is good' or 'the asset is bad') but can also see the history of what everyone before them did. In the human world, this setup is a recipe for 'informational cascades'—where people ignore their own private information and blindly follow the crowd, creating massive asset bubbles or sudden panics.
The Findings

items: AI is stubbornly rational: In the baseline setup, the LLM agents were remarkably rational. They relied heavily on their private signals rather than blindly following the herd. The share of rational or partially rational decisions in the AI lab was a staggering 97%, compared to just 65% for humans.

Zero stupid mistakes: While human participants made outright logical or arithmetic errors in 3.4% of their trades, the AI agents made exactly zero. They don't fat-finger their trades or get distracted by the office gossip.

The 'Maximise Profit' catch: Here is the kicker. When the researchers explicitly prompted the LLMs to 'maximise profits,' the AI agents did start herding. But they did it 'optimally'—using Bayesian updating to calculate that the crowd's actions actually contained valuable information. While this is technically rational, it means they still herd.

Human baggage: Despite being code, the LLMs still showed signs of human conditioning and bias inherited from their training data. They aren't cold, clinical calculators; they are mirrors of us, just with better maths.

content.text: The Key Quote

Our results show that AI agents make more rational decisions than humans, relying predominantly on private information over market trends. Increased reliance on AI-powered investment advice could therefore potentially lead to fewer asset price bubbles arising from animal spirits...
What to Skim vs. What to Read

If you aren't a hardcore quant, you can safely skim the mathematical proofs of Bayesian herding and the exact API prompt structures in the appendix. Instead, focus your attention on Section 3 (the experimental results) and Section 4 (the variations where they change the prompts to 'maximise profit'). That's where the real commercial juice is.
How It Connects to You

Whether you are in asset management, sales & trading, or quant research, you need to understand how market dynamics will change as more decision-making is outsourced to AI. If the market becomes dominated by AI agents, we might see fewer retail-driven 'meme stock' bubbles. However, we might also see a new kind of risk: highly synchronised, 'rational' panics where every model calculates the exact same Bayesian probabilities and rushes for the exit at the exact same millisecond.
What to Say at the Pub (or in an Interview)

If this comes up over a pint or in an interview, you can sound incredibly sharp by saying: 'The Fed actually ran a study showing that LLMs are far less prone to irrational herding than humans because they stick to their private signals. But there’s a catch—the moment you prompt them to maximise profit, they start herding optimally using Bayesian logic. So, instead of eliminating bubbles, we might just be trading human 'animal spirits' for highly synchronised, algorithmic flash crashes when all the models run the same maths at once.'
Our Take

It’s a brilliant paper because it exposes the flaw in the 'AI will make markets perfectly efficient' argument. In the real world, nobody prompts an investment AI to 'just be a standard participant.' Every hedge fund, asset manager, and retail broker will prompt their models to maximise profit. This means the 'rational, non-herding' baseline is a fantasy. We aren't curing the market of herding; we are just upgrading the herd from emotional sheep to highly efficient, Bayesian wolves. When the wind changes, they will still run together—only much, much faster.

content.text: The McNamara Fallacy: Why Your Spreadsheet is Lying to You

We’ve all been there. You’re sitting in a meeting room in the City, and some senior director is pointing at a dashboard where every line is going up and to the right. The metrics are green, the KPIs are ticked, and yet, deep down, everyone in the room knows the project is a total bin fire. This disconnect isn't just bad luck; it’s a classic psychological trap known as the McNamara Fallacy (or the Quantitative Fallacy).

The name comes from Robert McNamara, the US Secretary of Defense during the Vietnam War. Before that, McNamara was one of the legendary 'Whiz Kids' who turned Ford Motor Company around using rigorous statistical analysis. When he took over the Pentagon, he tried to run the war like a car factory. He obsessed over quantifiable metrics: enemy body counts, ammunition spent, and kill ratios. Because the numbers looked great on his charts, he concluded America was winning. But he completely ignored the unmeasurable stuff—like local political dynamics, guerrilla morale, and public sentiment. The result was a catastrophic strategic failure.
Sociologist Daniel Yankelovich neatly mapped out how this trap works in four steps:

items: Step 1: Measure whatever can be easily measured (e.g., headcount, hours billed, backtest Sharpe ratio). This is fine as far as it goes.
Step 2: Disregard what can't be easily measured, or give it an arbitrary quantitative value. This is artificial and misleading.
Step 3: Presume that what can't be measured easily isn't really important. This is blindness.
Step 4: Presume that what can't be measured easily doesn't actually exist. This is suicide.

content.text: In the City, this is happening everywhere right now, especially with the rush to adopt AI. Firms are proudly reporting that their new LLM tools have increased 'developer productivity' by 40% because they are measuring lines of code written per hour. But they are completely ignoring the unmeasurable: the subtle rise in technical debt, the loss of junior developer training, and the security vulnerabilities that only show up months later. They’ve optimised for the metric they can count, while ignoring the risk that actually matters.

Similarly, in M&A, deal teams often fall into this trap by evaluating target acquisitions purely on clean, quantifiable metrics like EBITDA, CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost), and LTV (Lifetime Value) because they fit neatly into a DCF model. They ignore the toxic culture, the fact that key engineers are about to quit, or that the brand's reputation is quietly rotting on Reddit. They buy the company, and it falls apart because they treated the unmeasurable as non-existent.
How to use this at work and in interviews:

items: In interviews: When you’re asked how you’d evaluate an investment target or a new trading strategy, don't just list the financial metrics. Say: 'I’d start with the quantitative data, but I’d actively map out the qualitative factors we might be ignoring to avoid the McNamara Fallacy—like management culture or regulatory tail risks.' It instantly marks you out as a mature, commercial thinker, not just a spreadsheet monkey.

In pitch decks: Include a slide or a section titled 'The Unquantifiables'. Explicitly list the critical factors that your model can't capture. It disarms the sceptics in the room and shows you actually understand the limits of your own data.

With your boss: When they are obsessing over a vanity metric (like 'number of client emails sent'), gently steer the conversation back to the qualitative outcome (the actual strength of the client relationship).

content.text: One line to remember:
If you only manage what you can measure, you will end up perfectly measuring your own decline.
